title: She loved much (Luke 7:36–50)
hook: a sinful woman washes his feet with tears at a dinner she wasn't invited to

segments.voice: Yesterday, a funeral stopped at the gate of Naim, and a mother got her son back. Your line was weep not. Who did you comfort? Day four hundred fifty-six, and a new week.

A dinner party in a nice house. The host is a Pharisee named Simon, a serious, respected man who has invited the new teacher everyone's talking about. The guests aren't sitting on chairs. They're reclining on couches, leaning on one elbow, feet stretched out behind them. Dinners like this were often semi-public: people from the town could drift in and stand along the walls to listen. And someone does. A woman the whole town knows as a sinner comes in carrying an alabaster jar of ointment. She hasn't been invited. She goes straight to the teacher's feet. Today, what she does there, and what he says about it.
screen: `A DINNER AT SIMON'S HOUSE.` → `GUESTS RECLINING, FEET BEHIND.` → `AN UNINVITED WOMAN WITH A JAR.`

segments.voice: She stands behind him, at his feet, and starts to cry. Her tears fall on his feet, so she wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours out the ointment. The room goes quiet. Simon thinks to himself: if this man were a prophet, he'd know what sort of woman is touching him. Jesus answers the thought with a story. Two men owe a lender money, one five hundred pence, one fifty. Neither can pay, so he forgives them both. Which will love him more? Simon answers, carefully: I suppose the one who was forgiven more. Right, says Jesus. Then he turns toward the woman but keeps talking to Simon. You gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with tears. You gave me no kiss; she hasn't stopped kissing my feet. You didn't anoint my head; she anointed my feet. And then the line: "Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, he loveth less." To her he says: "Thy faith hath made thee safe, go in peace." Simon isn't the villain here. He invited Jesus, listened, and answered honestly. The story is about two kinds of guests, and it asks which one we are. Luke never names the woman. For many centuries in the Western Church, after a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great, she was identified with Mary Magdalene. The Church's calendar since 1969 treats them as separate women, and the Gospel itself doesn't say. What it does say is clear: she couldn't stop loving because she knew how much she'd been forgiven.
screen: `TEARS, HAIR, KISSES, OINTMENT.` · `TWO DEBTORS, BOTH FORGIVEN.` · `NO WATER, NO KISS, NO OIL.` · `GO IN PEACE.` · then, large: `SHE HATH LOVED MUCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love without counting. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been forgiven: by God, if you pray, or by a friend, a parent, a partner who let something go. Remember how it felt when they didn't hold it over you. Let that settle in your body. Then think of one person you've been loving carefully, in measured amounts, keeping track. Picture giving them one thing today without counting: a kindness, an apology, an hour. If you pray, you can thank God for what you've been forgiven. The bell holds the time.
She loved much. The unnamed woman at Simon's dinner, whose tears and ointment showed how much she knew she'd been forgiven. Today's word.
Your line: she loved much. Today, give one kindness to someone without keeping track of what they owe you. Day four hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics connect this story with the sacrament of Penance, where sins are forgiven and the priest sends the penitent away in peace, and many pray with it as an examination of how much they have been forgiven.

fork.setup: you're the host. an uninvited woman with a bad reputation is weeping on your guest's feet. what do you think?
options: if he were a prophet, he'd know what she is.
she's showing the welcome I forgot to give.
someone should ask her to leave.
fork.reveal: Simon thinks the first. Jesus answers with a story, then shows him the second was true: no water, no kiss, no oil from the host.

original.note: Greek: she loved much. The verb is the agape word, love that gives.

trapdoor: what you thought: this is the story of Mary Magdalene washing Jesus' feet.
what it means: an unnamed woman, known as a sinner, shows great love because she knows how much she has been forgiven.
what a scholar hears: Gregory the Great joined her to Mary Magdalene in a sermon around 591; the 1969 calendar reform treats them as separate.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 7:47 and 7:50, and 'pence' for the debts in 7:41.
Gregory the Great's identification of the sinful woman with Mary Magdalene (Homily 33, c. 591) and the 1969 General Roman Calendar treating them separately: confirm dates and phrasing.
Semi-public dinners with townspeople along the walls is a common background note; confirm.
The fork's 'answer' is what Simon actually thought (the text's answer), not a moral recommendation.
